props.title: The Northmen
props.subtitle: Raiders, settlers and the words they left
props.subject: ship

say: In seven hundred and ninety three, raiders from Scandinavia attacked the monastery of Lindisfarne, on a small island off the coast of Northumbria. It was one of the richest and holiest places in England, and it had no walls.

props.title: A Shock to the Christian World

say: The news shocked Christian Europe. For the next seventy years, the raids came again and again. Fast ships, quick attacks, and then gone, back across the sea.

Then, in eight hundred and sixty five, everything changed. A huge force landed in East Anglia. The English chroniclers called it the great army. These men had not come to raid. They had come to conquer.
York fell in eight hundred and sixty six. East Anglia fell. Mercia was overrun. Kingdom after kingdom collapsed, until only one was left standing. Wessex.
Its king was a young man named Alfred. History would later call him Alfred the Great. But in the winter of eight hundred and seventy eight, he was very close to losing everything.

A surprise attack at Chippenham sent him running. Alfred hid in the marshes of Athelney, in Somerset, with a small band of men. For a few months, the whole future of the English language hid there with him.
In May, he struck back. At the battle of Edington, Alfred's army broke the Danes. Their leader, Guthrum, agreed to peace, and to be baptised.
England was split in two. The south and west stayed English. The north and east, under Danish law, became known as the Danelaw.

props.title: A King Who Chose English
props.subject: Books in the people's language
props.body: Alfred wanted free young men to learn to read in English. He had important Latin books translated into English, so that his people could read them.

say: Alfred did something unusual for his time. Most learning was in Latin. But Alfred wanted his people to read in their own language, and he had important books translated into English. The war made English a symbol of survival.
But the Danes did not leave. They settled, farmed and married. Their towns are still on the map. Derby. Whitby. Grimsby. That ending, by, is Old Norse for a farm or a village.

props.title: Borrowed from the Northmen
props.subject: Everyday words
props.body: Sky. Egg. Knife. Window, from vindauga, the wind eye. Law. Ugly. Husband.

say: And their words moved into English. Sky. Egg. Knife. Law. Ugly. Husband. Even window, from the Norse vindauga, the wind's eye, a hole in the roof to let the smoke out.

props.title: The Words You Use Every Minute

say: The Norse even changed the smallest words. They, them and their all come from Old Norse. You probably say them hundreds of times a day, and every time, you are speaking Viking.
Sometimes, English kept both versions. Shirt is the Old English word. Skirt is its Norse cousin. They started as the same word, and ended up as two different pieces of clothing.
And in the end, the Danes took the crown itself. In ten sixteen, Cnut became king of England. Danish kings ruled until ten forty two, when an English king returned to the throne.
But peace would not last. In ten sixty six, two foreign armies would sail for England in the same autumn. One came from Norway. The other came from Normandy. And only one of them would win.
